analysis.one_liner: Cuts guaranteed monopoly sales rights for rare-disease drugs from seven years to four.
analysis.headline: The House Energy and Commerce Committee approved the bill by voice vote in September 1994, but it never received a floor vote in the House or Senate before the Congress ended in January 1995.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the 1983 Orphan Drug Act, the first company to win approval for a drug treating a rare disease (fewer than 200,000 U.S. patients) gets seven years of exclusive marketing rights, blocking competitors entirely. This bill would cut that monopoly to four years, with a three-year extension only for drugs the government determines have genuinely limited sales potential. It would also let a second company sell the same rare-disease drug when both firms were developing it at the same time, take away exclusivity if a disease turns out to affect more than 200,000 people, and extend federal research grants for rare-disease drug development.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients with rare diseases, who would face competition for these drugs sooner and potentially lower prices; and smaller biotech and generic firms that could enter a rare-disease market once the shortened exclusivity ended or when they had developed a rival drug in parallel with the first company.

how_it_helps.text: Shortens the guaranteed market exclusivity for approved orphan drugs from seven years to four years, allowing competing products to enter three years sooner [S3][S4].

Allows a second company to market the same rare-disease drug if it applied for designation within six months of the first company's designation, started trials within twelve months, and filed its application within twelve months — ending a winner-take-all rule for drugs developed simultaneously [S3][S4].
Removes exclusivity if the designated disease is later found to affect more than 200,000 people, closing a way for companies to keep monopoly rights on drugs with larger patient populations [S3][S4].
Extends and increases federal research grant funding for rare-disease drug development, to $20 million in 1995 rising to $30 million by 1997 [S3][S4].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug makers holding orphan drug designations, who would lose three years of exclusive, competition-free sales on each qualifying drug and face new competition from simultaneous developers; and, indirectly, any rare-disease research that the industry argues depends on longer exclusivity to be profitable.

drawbacks.text: Shorter exclusivity weakens the core incentive of the Orphan Drug Act: the monopoly period is what makes it profitable for companies to develop drugs for very small patient populations that would otherwise be abandoned, and cutting it to four years risks fewer rare-disease drugs being developed [S3].

The 'limited commercial potential' test that governs which drugs get the three-year extension is left to regulations the Health and Human Services Secretary would write, based on sales revenue or other factors — a judgment-heavy standard that would be contested by industry and could be applied inconsistently [S4].

The bill grandfathers existing drugs — applications submitted or approved before March 1, 1994 keep the full seven-year exclusivity — so patients would see no relief on drugs already on the market [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real problem: the Orphan Drug Act, designed to rescue abandoned drugs for tiny patient groups, had also granted seven-year monopolies on drugs with substantial sales, keeping prices high. Cutting exclusivity to four years with an escape valve for genuinely unprofitable drugs is a reasonable rebalance. The honest cost is the incentive argument — the same monopoly that overpays patients on commercially viable orphan drugs is what keeps money flowing into research on non-viable ones, and a shorter period means less of it.

outcome.mechanism: The House committee approved it by voice vote and it was placed on the House calendar in late September 1994, but the session ended before the House or Senate ever voted on it.

narrative.text: Waxman introduced the bill on August 1, 1994, with the Energy and Commerce Committee referring it the same day [S1][S6].
The committee held a markup on August 5, ordered the bill reported as amended by voice vote, and formally reported it on September 26, 1994 [S6].

The bill was placed on the Union Calendar (Calendar No. 410) on September 26, 1994, awaiting floor action that never came; the record shows no House vote, no Senate action, and the 103rd Congress ended January 3, 1995 [S6][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name orphan drug makers, who kept the full seven-year exclusivity on future rare-disease drugs and faced no new competition rules or grant money. Rare-disease patients kept paying monopoly prices for the drugs they use.

for.name: Rep. Henry Waxman
for.role: House Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee chair; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and steered it through the committee he chaired a subcommittee on, which reported it as amended by voice vote.

for.name: Rep. Gerry Studds
for.what_they_did: Joined Waxman in introducing the bill — the bill's only cosponsor.

for.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
for.what_they_did: Held a markup on August 5, 1994, ordered the bill reported as amended by voice vote, and reported it with a committee report on September 26.

against.name: Pharmaceutical manufacturers
against.role: Brand-name drug industry holding orphan drug exclusivities
against.what_they_did: Opposed shortening the seven-year orphan drug exclusivity period, the core industry benefit of the 1983 Orphan Drug Act; the bill's action history records no floor vote after it was calendared.

against.name: 103rd Congress
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to a floor vote in either chamber before the session ended in January 1995.

sides.party_line_note: Both sponsor and cosponsor were Democrats and the committee reported the bill by voice vote, so the record shows no party-split vote; there is no roll-call data on where Republicans stood.

industries.note: The bill cuts their guaranteed seven-year competition-free period to four years, allows rival firms that developed the same drug in parallel to sell it, and strips exclusivity when a disease exceeds 200,000 patients. That competition would lower prices for patients but shorten monopoly revenue for the companies.

industries.industry: Smaller biotech and follow-on drug firms
industries.note: Firms that developed a rare-disease drug simultaneously with the incumbent, or that could sell after a four-year exclusivity, would gain market access they are currently barred from.
The bill extends the federal Orphan Products research grant program and roughly doubles to triples its annual funding levels through 1997.
